1:
The opening notice is read for its emphasis and for its date. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) finds the weight laid on all characteristic of a writer compiling after the disruption of the kingdom; John Gill (reformed) makes the contrast from both ends, since David was not at first king over all but only over Judah and Solomon’s successors were not so after the division, and connects it to the wisdom of the preceding chapter, so that he reigned by the consent of all and in the hearts of all. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) adds that he was a king in the sense of doing the work and duty of one. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) date the list to the middle of the reign, since two officers named married daughters of Solomon, which they could not have done till his later years.

The order of the list is itself treated as evidence. Ellicott notes that whereas in David’s lists the captain of the host stands first, here both military offices are preceded by the peaceful offices of priest, scribes and recorder; Keil and Delitzsch observe the same from the other side, that the first of the princes is not the commander-in-chief, as under David’s warlike reign, but, suiting Solomon’s peaceful rule, the administrator of the kingdom.

What the title given to Azariah means is the chapter’s first real dispute. Keil and Delitzsch deny it is the priesthood at all: the word is not the priest but the administrator of the kingdom, the king’s representative before the people, the article marking him first among the confidential counsellors. They reject the construal of the Vulgate, Luther and Thenius, which against the accents joins the word genitivally to the patronymic. Ellicott goes the other way for this verse while conceding the wider usage: the word keeps traces of the old time when priesthood and headship of a family were united, and so was applied to princes, being given to the sons of David where the parallel in Chronicles paraphrases it as chief about the king. But here, he says, there is every reason for the usual sense, Azariah having been a prince before he succeeded to the high priesthood, and the mingling of priestly and princely functions being characteristic of the time. He holds the title to be given here by anticipation, since the text says expressly a little below that Zadok and Abiathar were the priests.

That notice raises its own problem, since Abiathar had been deposed. Keil and Delitzsch call it strange that he is named as priest beside Zadok, say no subsequent pardon can be imagined, and accept Theodoret’s as the only possible explanation: that Solomon stripped him of the office but not of the priestly dignity, which was hereditary and not conferred by appointment. Ellicott reaches the same result by another route: though disgraced and practically deposed he was still theoretically priest, the priesthood being properly for life, much as Annas is called high priest in the Gospels.

Two smaller identifications close the section. On the father of Zabud, Keil and Delitzsch deny Thenius’s view that the prophet is meant and take him for David’s son of that name, which makes Azariah and Zabud nephews of Solomon; Ellicott argues the same from the book’s own habit, that Nathan the prophet always has his title appended where he is first named. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) glosses Zabud as perhaps what we should call premier, and remarks that none of these men were princes in the common acceptation of the word. Henry draws the continuity out: several are the same who served in his father’s time, and when sons inherit their father’s power it is a piece of respect to his memory to employ whom he employed and trust whom he trusted — whereas many pride themselves on being the reverse of their good parents.
7:
What these twelve men were is disputed. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) deny they were chamberlains or administrators of the royal domains, as Michaelis and Ewald held, since officers of that kind appear in Chronicles under a different title; they are rather chief tax-collectors, levying the king’s duties, which in the East consisted then as now mostly of the produce of the land rather than of money payments as in the West, and delivering them at the royal kitchen. They add that Josephus’s rendering of the term by governors and generals cannot be used, as Thenius uses it, to infer that they exercised a kind of government, being merely a subjective conjecture. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) agrees it denotes the collection of revenue, mostly in kind, for the court, household and guards, but allows that it may have included the management of the royal domain lands as well. John Gill (reformed) explains the number: it answers not to the twelve tribes, since each seems to have held only particular places within a tribe, but to the twelve months, in which each took his turn. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) observes only that providing daily for such a household, each man for his month, was no easy task.

That five of the twelve are given by patronymic and not by name is explained four ways. Ellicott calls it curious and lays it to some defect in the archives from which the chapter is evidently drawn. Keil and Delitzsch think it very improbable that proper names dropped out five times, as Clericus and Michaelis supposed, and are left with the assumption that these men bore their fathers’ names with the prefix as their own, on the analogy of a similar name in Chronicles — conceding that one of the five looks very strange so taken. Gill supposes the fathers’ names were given because the fathers were well known. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) reads it as usage rather than as a problem: they are named by their surnames, as great men commonly call their servants.

How far the districts answer to the old tribal lands is the section’s substantive question. Ellicott counts nine west and three east of Jordan and finds they coincide only in a few cases with the lands assigned to the tribes; he thinks much of the tribal division had by this time probably become obsolete, though Chronicles shows it still in force for chieftainship over men and for the levy in war. Gill reaches the same conclusion from the other direction, that the officers held particular places within tribes rather than tribes entire. On the two officers married into the royal house Ellicott infers that the office must have been one of high importance and dignity; Keil and Delitzsch identify one of them as probably a son of David’s brother and so Solomon’s cousin as well as his son-in-law, and use both marriages to date the whole list to the middle of the reign. Henry turns it to the daughters’ credit: no disparagement to marry men of business, and a better match with Israelite officers of their father’s court than with sons of princes who were strangers to the covenant of promise. Gill adds a conjecture of his own, that one officer may have been a son of Hushai the Archite, David’s friend, and promoted for his father’s sake.

Two difficulties of detail close the list. On the apparent contradiction that one man is called the only officer in a land where two others are also stationed, Henry and Gill give the same solution, that the other two depended on him and were subordinate to him. Keil and Delitzsch add a textual charge, that the Septuagint arbitrarily interpolated a word before one place-name, which Thenius naturally takes under his protection without considering that it yields no sense unless another word precedes it.
20:
The note of national prosperity is taken by four witnesses as fulfilled promise and by one as decline. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) read the numbering as the sand of the sea as showing that the word given to the patriarchs had been kept, and the extent of the rule as showing the other half of it kept too, that the seed should possess the gates of its enemies. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) presses it further: the description specifies not merely wealth but the fact that Israel were now a dominant race relieved of all burden of labour and ruling over subject peoples reduced to serfship, and that now for the first time they entered full possession of the territory promised at the Conquest — it was otherwise afterwards, as the complaints brought to Rehoboam show. John Gill (reformed) assigns causes, great fruitfulness in their families with neither pestilence nor wars to lessen their number, and reads the multitude as an emblem of Christ’s spiritual subjects. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) takes the whole as a type of the Messiah’s kingdom answering the seventy-second Psalm, and notes that Solomon invaded no man’s property, as the manner of the king had been, so that what men had they could call their own. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) alone reads the eating and drinking and making merry against the grain: they were very comfortable, very rich, very merry and very corrupt, and this full feeding and dissipation led to a total corruption of manners.

How the empire is to be understood divides them. Clarke maps it simply, Euphrates east, the Philistines west, Egypt south, infers Syria, Damascus, Moab and Ammon as tributaries, and concludes with Calmet that Solomon possessed all the land covenanted to Abraham. Ellicott is more careful about what the dominion was: as in all ancient Eastern empires it represented not an organised monarchy but the supremacy of a dominant kingdom over tributaries gathered round, so that it would rise rapidly and as rapidly fall to pieces; it was the fruit of the warlike energy of the two preceding reigns but was sustained less by military power than by the peaceful forces of wealth and policy, and was largely dependent on Solomon’s personal ascendancy; and he holds the Syrian kingdoms, like Tyre, to have been allies on a footing of some dependence rather than tributaries proper. Both he and Keil and Delitzsch read the phrase rendered on this side the river as meaning literally the further side, reckoned from Babylon, and both draw the same inference from it, that the book was composed in exile or at least when the Babylonish empire governed the geography of the East. Keil and Delitzsch add a textual caution: most commentators supply a missing preposition from the parallel in Chronicles, but it is improbable that so indispensable a word dropped out, and unnecessary to supply it, since the preposition of the preceding clause can be repeated in thought.

The daily provision sets off the chapter’s one measurable disagreement, and the spread is nearly twentyfold. Henry reckons the flour and meal would richly serve three thousand men, and reports Carellus at above four thousand eight hundred. Ellicott, allowing that the measure is variously estimated between forty-two and eighty-six gallons, will say only that the quantity indicates probably several thousands in the household, court and guard. Keil and Delitzsch calculate from Thenius’s value that ninety measures would yield some twenty-eight thousand pounds of bread, and at two pounds a head put fourteen thousand persons at court. Clarke reports the two highest figures of all, Vilalpandus at not less than forty-eight thousand six hundred and Calvisius at fifty-four thousand, and accounts for them by supposing the guards included, each receiving a ration from the king’s store. Gill measures the vessel itself at Bishop Cumberland’s seventy-five wine gallons and somewhat more.
29:
The three gifts are distinguished before they are praised. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) separates understanding, which is high intellectual power, and largeness of heart, which is capacity of knowledge, from the higher gift of wisdom to which both are means only — the one the capacity within, the other its education from without. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) offers three readings of largeness of heart in turn: the intellectual powers, the heart being often put for those; or courage and the assurance with which he delivered his determinations; or a disposition to do good with knowledge, being free and communicative, as free of his learning as he was of his meat. He then turns the gift into a warning: lose the sense of the need of revelation and this consciousness of wisdom may become a self-idolatry in which the mind prides itself on having pierced to the secret of being, holds that such knowledge sets it above ordinary law and duty, and delights in contemplation rather than in active energy and devotion. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) is content with Lord Bacon’s figure, which he calls happy and correct: as the sand on the shore encloses a great body of waters, so Solomon’s mind contained an ocean of knowledge. John Gill (reformed) insists it came neither from acuteness of genius nor from industry but by the gift of God, the fountain of all understanding.

Who the four named rivals were is the chapter’s last real dispute, and it turns on chronology. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) identify them with the sons of Zerach in Chronicles, the names agreeing but one, whose difference they lay to a copyist’s error; they support it by the title Ezrahite borne by two of them in the Psalms, derived from the family name of Zerach lengthened by a prosthetic letter, while conceding that both men were Levites. Ellicott grants the coincidence remarkable enough to suggest it, then refuses it: the passage implies rivals contemporary with Solomon, not a family generations earlier, and a Heman and an Ethan are known who were set by David over the service of song and called Ezrahites in two psalm titles, the one designated the king’s seer in the words of the Lord. Clarke refuses it on the same ground, Zerah having flourished long before Solomon; Henry simply takes the men as the Levites whom David employed in the temple music. Both notice that the patronymic of the other two may be no name at all, the word signifying dance or music, so that they may have been masters of music — which would make the comparison one of poetry rather than philosophy.

How little survives of the three thousand proverbs and the thousand and five songs is counted exactly. Clarke finds only about nine hundred distinct proverbs in the book bearing the name, and no more than six hundred and fifty if its first nine chapters are not Solomon’s. Keil and Delitzsch call what we have a comparatively small portion, probably a selection of the best; Henry will not go so far, holding it uncertain whether the proverbs we have were any part of the three thousand at all. Ellicott, deriving the word for proverb from a root signifying comparison and distinguishing four senses of it, says the two collected series fall far short of the number given. Gill accounts for the loss: these were spoken and not written, taken from his lips and spread by hearers, and in time lost, whereas the book, written under inspiration, was preserved. On the songs the two part company: Keil and Delitzsch allow two psalms besides the Song of Songs which bear his name and justly bear it, while Clarke holds one of those two to be more properly a psalm of direction left him by his father about building the temple.
